1:
Why a register of Esau belongs here is the first thing several of them answer. Gill gives four — Esau was Isaac's son, whose burial has just been told; his descendants are noticed so often later that this genealogy illustrates those places; the promise to Abraham and the oracle to Rebekah about two nations in her womb are seen taking effect; and so is Isaac's blessing on him. He adds a fifth from Maimonides which he thinks the principal one: Amalek, a branch of the family, lay under an express sentence of destruction, so the rest had to be described particularly lest they perish with him. Keil and Delitzsch reason from the structure. Esau too had a divine promise, and his tribe's future was woven into the paternal blessing, so its growth into a nation gets a section of its own, standing by the book's plan before the generations of Jacob and subdivided by its own headings. They quote Delitzsch on the parting: the brothers shook hands once more over their father's corpse, and their paths thenceforth diverged to meet no more. Clarke says the generations are set down so exactly to show how exactly God kept his promise to this son, and that the Horite line is appended because the two families afterwards became blended.

Henry and Wesley hear a reproach in the surname, which keeps up the memory of the foolish bargain, the birthright sold for red pottage. Henry thinks that enough to explain why this family is dismissed so briefly: if men do a wrong thing they must thank themselves when it is remembered against them long afterwards. Three wives, he notes, and by all three only five sons, where many a man has more by one; God often disappoints those who take crooked ways to build a house, though here the promise prevailed. He also weighs the brothers: in outward prosperity the children of the covenant are often behind and those outside it get the start, and it must have tried Israel's faith to hear of the pomp of Edom's kings while they were bond-slaves in Egypt — but men who look for great things from God must wait.

Calvin turns the catalogue into a comment on its worth. Esau was an alien from the Church, yet as Isaac's son he had a temporal blessing, and Moses celebrates his race — a commemoration, Calvin says, resembling an honourable burial. Their precedence was a bubble under the figure of this world; Esau is set up as on a lofty theatre, and because no condition lasts outside the kingdom of God the pomp goes off like a scene shifted on a stage. The Spirit meant to testify that Isaac's prophecy had not been empty, and having shown its effect draws our eyes away, as though casting a veil over it, that we may attend to the race of Jacob. On the three wives he will not let a good outcome excuse the practice: polygamy is not approved, nor impure lust; what deserves admiration is a goodness that gave a good issue to evil beginnings, against the order of nature.

Ellicott opens with a warning. The section abounds in difficulties, too often aggravated by commentators determined to make Scripture bend to their notions of what it ought to be rather than accept it as it is. His test case is the list of kings: no prophetical passage but a dry genealogical table, whose plain sense — that when it was written there were kings in Israel — commentators evade in ways painful to read and apt only to harden sceptics. Nor will he call the closing lists interpolations: completing a genealogy was ordinary, and the prophets had authority to add what was needed — he instances the note about Rachel's pillar standing unto this day, and dates those documents to about the time the Books of Samuel were composed.
2:
The wives are named differently here from before, and the two who notice take opposite views of how much that matters; Keil and Delitzsch record the fact and pass on. Clarke lists the changes — the Aholibamah here appears earlier as Judith, Adah there as Bashemath, this Bashemath as Mahalath elsewhere — and declines to spend time on them: they cannot easily be accounted for, are not worth detaining a reader, and the same persons in Scripture often bear different names. Gill adds only that these were daughters of Canaan, of the posterity of cursed Canaan — most of them, though not all, one wife coming of Ishmael's family.

Ellicott builds on what Clarke waves away. Two names for one woman is unusual, but this one was a Hittite whose name in her own tongue was neither Adah nor Bashemath; since Adah means ornament and Bashemath sweet-scented, both may be endearments formed from it. As for Aholibamah, commonly identified with Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite — her grandfather Zibeon is called a Horite further down, the letters for Hivite and Horite differ only in one stroke, and errors in copying names are constant. He concludes she was a Horite and a different woman from Judith, and then finds the order of the list falling into place. Judith seems to have had no children, which tempted Esau to marry again; Adah stands first as the first wife who bore sons, her Eliphaz holding the primogeniture, and Aholibamah third because taken last. The same marriage explains why a Horite pedigree is inserted here, and why Esau took Horite land: marrying a duke's daughter on some expedition into Seir gained him ducal rank and friendly terms with part of that people. Excepting the Semites, he adds, no race in Palestine stood so high as the Hittites and none so low as the Horites — a lowness inferred not from their cave-dwelling, the country being well suited to it, but from their absence from the table of nations.

The last of these sons dates the migration for Ellicott. Esau appears in Seir with an armed band when Jacob returns from Padan-aram, but his home was still at Hebron for twenty-two years more, and Aholibamah had plainly been taken there, bearing three sons in Canaan. Only after Isaac died did Seir draw him off with his share of the wealth, leaving Hebron to Jacob, who came down from Eder to take his fathers' homestead — so the birthright came to Jacob by Esau's own act.

One phrase here contradicts a later one, and Clarke sets out the remedies. Anah is here and again below the daughter of Zibeon, yet further on the son. The Samaritan, Greek and Syriac read son, which Houbigant and Kennicott hold the true text; others refer daughter to Aholibamah, making her Anah's daughter and Zibeon's granddaughter. Clarke prefers the first, which brings every mention into agreement.

Ellicott finds a second slip in the next name. The Samaritan reads Mahalath here and in three other places, as the earlier chapter does, and he has little doubt that is right; but the versions side with the Masoretic text, so the error must be very old. Being of Semitic stock, she would have had her own name and no second rendering.

Two of the sons draw a note from Gill. Jerome and the Targum of Jonathan make Eliphaz the friend who visited Job, though Gill thinks that man his grandson, being called the Temanite. And the Korah here turns up again among the sons of Eliphaz: Jarchi takes them for one man and a bastard, got by Eliphaz on his father's wife; Aben Ezra reports the opinion that there were two, then argues for one — Aholibamah's son, reckoned among Eliphaz's because he lived among them, or because his mother died young and Adah reared him with her own, as with Michal's children.
6:
What Esau took is listed; what is left out Gill marks — the wives and sons are named already, but of the daughters neither names nor number. Why he went is where the readings pull hard against each other. Clarke takes the withdrawal for dignified conduct, of a character with the rest of his behaviour toward his brother: the two had lived together in Canaan on the friendliest footing since Jacob's return, and Esau left the better country to him and went back voluntarily to a far less fruitful one. Calvin denies the motive. Esau was too proud and ferocious ever to seem his brother's inferior, and nothing was further from his mind than Jacob's welfare; he moved for the advantage he expected, and Moses, ignoring the man's design, commends the secret providence that drove him into exile so that the land might be left free. God led the blind man by the hand, lest he settle where his own servant was to be; so it often falls out that the wicked do the elect good against their intention, furthering the salvation of men whose ruin they have desired. Even the vagueness of the phrase is evidence: Esau departed simply into the country, his plan unsettled and one place tried after another until Seir offered itself — he went out, as the saying is, à son aventure. Ellicott confines himself to the Hebrew: into a land away from the face.

Wesley traces the move in stages. Esau had begun settling among his wife's relations before Jacob came back from Padan-aram, sent there most likely by Isaac, to clear Jacob's way to the promised land; while Isaac lived he kept property in Canaan, and only after the death took his share of the estate and withdrew for good — partly because Jacob held the promise, partly because two households thriving at that rate would not both have room.

Room is the reason the text gives. Gill compares the parting of Abraham and Lot; Ellicott calls this separation as inevitable and quite ordinary among nomads, since a tribe grows only as far as its district will feed it, after which part of it must go. The pressure was worse because both were sojourners among tribes that claimed the soil — which may itself have pointed Esau toward Seir, where he ranked as a duke in right of Aholibamah. Maimonides, he notes, thought Esau had hunted and perhaps raided there, but lacked the strength to seize the country until Isaac's death multiplied his retainers.

The mountain's name sets Gill sorting explanations. He rejects Josephus, who derives it from Esau's own shaggy hair, and still more R. Abraham Seba's satyrs and hairy demons haunting the place; he prefers Seir the Horite who lived there, or the look of the mountain itself, rugged as shaggy hair with its bushes and brambles — which sets it neatly against Mount Halak nearby, the bald one, bare of shrubs. He adds that the Targum of Jonathan calls it Mount Gabla, and a district of Edom went by the name Gobolites, perhaps the Gebal of Scripture; and he has Esau drive out the Horites and seize the mount once matters with his brother were amicably settled. Ellicott describes the country: a limestone chain veined with basalt, running from the south end of the Dead Sea to the Gulf of Elath, much of it too stony to bear anything and the rest fertile in figs and pomegranates rather than corn, with summers cooled by winds and cold winters, and its border only fifty or sixty miles from Hebron. Wesley closes on the theology of it: God's word takes place whatever opposition is made, and those who opposed it are obliged sooner or later to yield. Esau had struggled for Canaan and now retires to Seir, God's counsels standing sure concerning the times before appointed and the bounds of our habitation.
9:
Two things about this list Henry and Wesley fasten on, in nearly the same words. The first is what the register withholds. Only the names of Esau's sons and grandsons are set down, not their history, because it is the church whose records Moses is keeping and not the records of those outside it; the elders who lived by faith are the ones who obtained a good report, and it is Sion that produces the men of renown, not Seir. Nor does the line run past the third and fourth generation — the very names of everyone after are buried in oblivion — whereas the pedigree of the Israelites, who were to inherit Canaan and from whom the promised and holy seed was to come, is drawn out as far as there was occasion for it: through every tribe until Canaan was divided among them, and through the royal line until Christ came.

The second is the title. These sons and grandsons are called dukes, and both take them for military commanders with soldiers under them, since Esau's family lived by the sword. Henry draws the moral out further than Wesley does. Titles of honour, he observes, have been older outside the church than in it, Esau's sons being dukes while Jacob's were still plain shepherds — which is no argument against Christians using such titles, but a good reason for not overvaluing anyone on account of them, there being an honour that comes from God and a name in his house worth infinitely more. Edomites may be dukes among men; Israelites indeed are made kings and priests to our God. Both then note the dukedoms themselves, households of children and servants large enough to be counted as such, and both draw the same comparison: God had promised to multiply Jacob and enrich him, yet it is Esau who increases and grows rich first. Henry adds that it is nothing new for the men of this world to be full of children and have their bellies filled with hidden treasure, and both close by saying that the promise to Jacob began to work late, lasted longer, and had its complete accomplishment in the spiritual Israel.

On the heading itself Ellicott and Calvin read the same phrase differently in emphasis. Ellicott points out that the Hebrew says father of Edom, and that since Esau was himself the man Edom the word must here mean the country he colonised. Calvin takes the second name as pointing forward to the posterity called Idumeans, and thinks Moses styles him father of a celebrated and famous people on purpose, to show what God had bestowed on him for his father Isaac's sake. Tracing the prophecy into Esau's progeny serves a further end, he argues: if the promise flourished so mightily toward a stranger, how much more powerfully must it work toward the children to whom the adoption and the inheritance of grace belong? Esau was an obscure man and a sojourner in that country; whence then should rulers suddenly spring from him and a great people flourish, unless the blessing that came out of Isaac's mouth was confirmed by the event? And he did not take that desert unopposed, for a people of no ignoble name held Mount Seir before him — Moses says plainly that the earlier inhabitants were mighty, so that a stranger could hardly have won such power without divine help.

Keil and Delitzsch attend to the word behind duke. Aluphim was the distinguishing title of the Edomite and Horite phylarchs, applied to Jewish heads of tribes only incidentally and late, in Zechariah, and probably derived from the word for a thousand, which stands elsewhere for families. Gill fills in one name as the list opens: Teman, the firstborn of Eliphaz, gave his name to the city of Teman in Idumea, which is why Eliphaz himself is called the Temanite.
12:
A concubine's name is enough to set the commentators working. Gill reports that Timna was sister to Lotan, the eldest son of Seir the Horite, and then lays out two rabbinic attempts to reconcile her with the Timna who turns up among the sons of Eliphaz and with the duke of that name further down the chapter. Gerundinsis has the concubine bear Amalek, conceive again, and die in childbirth, the father calling the second child by her name to keep her memory alive. Jarchi takes a stranger road: Eliphaz lay with Lotan's mother, the wife of Seir the Horite, and Timna was born of that; when she grew up she became his concubine, so that she was at once his daughter and his concubine.

Clarke takes the relationship as the historical hinge. Timna's being Lotan's sister shows how the family of Esau and the Horites came to be intermixed, and that intermixture, he suggests, later gave Esau's sons their pretext for seizing the land and driving out its old inhabitants. Of the son she bore he says only what the rest of Scripture says: Amalek was father of the Amalekites, afterwards bitter enemies of the Jews, and a people God commanded to be exterminated outright.

Ellicott will not have the descent so simple. Balaam calls Amalek the beginning of nations, a phrase implying precedence and nobility, and a field of the Amalekite has already been mentioned much earlier in the book; a race of that standing can hardly have sprung from the concubine of Eliphaz. It was besides one of the most widely spread peoples of antiquity, holding the whole country from Shur on the border of Egypt to Havilah in Arabia Felix. His solution is a fusion. Some of the Horites were probably absorbed into the Amalekites, much as the Kenezites under Caleb were absorbed into Judah; and the Amalekites whom the Simeonites afterwards smote in Mount Seir, according to Chronicles, are the ones this Amalek founded — for he is called a duke here, and a duke's descendants would hold a district of their own, exactly as each son of Jacob had a territory named after him. In that district the chiefs would be Semites of Esau's line and the bulk of the people a blend of Horite and Amalekite. Their absence from the table of nations he thinks no difficulty at all: whatever Balaam made of them, Israel never regarded them as a nation, only as a hateful horde of plunderers.

The remaining names Gill passes over quickly — Reuel, another son of Esau, with four sons of his own, and then the sons Aholibamah bore.
15:
What a duke was, three of them try to fix. Gill reports Ben Melech's distinction — a king is crowned and a duke is not — but prefers Jarchi's reading of the word as head of a family, which fits the context: the men already named had large households of which they were heads and governors, and the title is now attached to each of them in turn. Clarke goes at it through the languages. Duke is the Latin dux, a captain or leader; the Hebrew alluph means the same, and since the word also stands for a thousand — a leading number — the alluphey were probably so called from commanding a thousand men, like the chiliarchs among the Greeks and the centurions among the Romans, whose name comes from the word for a hundred. He notes that this ducal government was the earliest form among the Idumeans, and counts fourteen dukes to Esau: seven descended from Adah, four from Bashemath, three from Aholibamah. Ellicott makes the office territorial rather than military. Alluph means a tribal prince, and eleph, a thousand, was used much as our own word hundred once was for a division of country — a district large enough to hold a thousand grown men, where the Saxon hundred held a hundred homesteads. Each prince would govern one such district, assigned to him and his seed as a possession.

Then comes a name that ought not to be where it stands, and Clarke states the case against it at length on Dr Kennicott's authority. Eliphaz was Esau's son by Adah and had six sons, none of them Korah; Korah was Esau's own son by Aholibamah, and is properly listed as such a few verses later. Some copyist, therefore, inserted duke Korah into this verse, and both the Samaritan text and the Samaritan version are free of the insertion. Everything considered, Clarke inclines to think the words were never in the text. Ellicott agrees in a sentence: the Samaritan Pentateuch rightly omits the name, its bearer being a son of the Horite wife. Gill declines to cut it. He notes the omission in the Samaritan and the absence of any such son from the earlier list, then offers Gerundinsis's identification of this Korah with the Timna reckoned among Eliphaz's sons, whom his father called by that name — or else supposes a grandson of Eliphaz.

Ellicott finds a reason for the shape of the list as a whole. Aholibamah's three sons are themselves dukes, whereas the other wives are represented only by grandsons; and that is probably because she came of the ruling family of Seir, so that her sons took command of Horite districts and tribes in her right.

Keil and Delitzsch look ahead to the people already in the land. The Horite is the dweller in caves, the Greek rendering it troglodyte, and caves abound in the mountains of Edom; once an independent nation, they were afterwards in part exterminated and in part subjugated.
20:
A second genealogy opens inside the first, and everyone pauses to say why. Gill notes the Targum's added word — these inhabited the land before it belonged to Esau's posterity and took his name — and points out that the Horites were there as far back as Abraham's day. Their name he derives from their living underground in holes and caves, with which the further part of Edom abounds; they are the people the Greeks call Trogloditae, and Jarchi reports from the Rabbins that they were expert judges of ground and knew what would carry olives and what vines. Two reasons Gill gives for the insertion: to show who held the country before Esau's sons succeeded them, and because of the intermarriages that eased the transfer — Esau himself married a daughter of Anah son of Zibeon, and Eliphaz took Lotan's sister Timna. Clarke says the same more briefly, that these were the original inhabitants of what was called the land of the Horites and afterwards of the Idumeans once Esau's descendants had driven them out. Ellicott adds his own pair of reasons: the list contains Aholibamah's own pedigree, but chiefly it is here because Horite and Edomite were in time fused into one people.

Henry and Wesley take the intermarriage as an indictment. The Horite genealogy stands in the middle of the Edomite one not merely to light up the story but as a standing reproach to the Edomites for marrying into that stock, by which they probably learned their ways and corrupted themselves. Esau had sold his birthright, lost his blessing and allied himself with the Hittites, and so his posterity and the sons of Seir are reckoned together here — men who treacherously desert God's church, Henry says, are justly numbered with those who were never in it, and apostate Edomites stand on the same ground as accursed Horites.

Both then single out one man from the list to make a kinder point. Anah fed his father's asses and is nevertheless called a duke, from which Henry draws two morals: those who expect to rise high should begin low, and an honourable descent should keep no man from honest work, nor mean work hinder his advancement. He was industrious, and ingenious with it, and successful — he found mules in the wilderness, or, as some read the word, waters, hot baths; and men diligent in their business, Henry adds, sometimes find more than they were looking for.

The Horite princes raise a question of dating. Clarke observes that Horites and Esau's descendants were mixed together in one land, and cites Calmet's remark that setting this verse beside the later list shows princes of Seir both in Seir and in Edom, which obliges us to treat the two lines as contemporary. Keil and Delitzsch render the closing formula flatly, the princes of the Horites according to their princes. Gill counts the sons — Dishon, Ezer and Dishan making seven with the four already named — and, on the next generation, thinks Hori took his name from the tribe as a whole while his brother appears elsewhere as Homam; Shobal, the second son, he gives five sons.

One name in that list needs disentangling, and Ellicott does it. The Timna here is not the Timna of the earlier verse. This one is sister to Lotan and so to Zibeon, the grandfather of Esau's wife, whereas the other was concubine to Esau's grandson and four generations her junior.
24:
One clause in this list has defeated everybody, and Clarke sets out the wreckage. Jerome, who renders it warm springs, remarked that there were as many opinions about the word as there were commentators, and Clarke's survey bears him out. The Greek turns it into what looks like a man's name, spelt differently in different copies. The Syriac gives waters, its translator having evidently read the Hebrew for water, the first two letters transposed. Onkelos makes it giants, or strong and powerful men. The Samaritan text and version both have the Emim, a warlike people on the Horite border. The Targum of Jonathan ben Uzziel is circumstantial: this is the Anah who put the onager to the tame ass and in time found mules produced between them. Kimchi has Zibeon for both father and brother of Anah, and Anah so bent on heterogeneous mixtures that he set asses and horses to breed; Jarchi agrees.

Against all of these Clarke sets Bochart, who argued for the Emim on four grounds — that the verb never means to invent but to light upon something already there; that mules are called by quite another word in Scripture; that Anah was pasturing asses and not horses; and that no mule is mentioned in Palestine before the days of David — and who piled up passages where finding a people means joining battle with them. Gusset went over Bochart's case and came back to mules; Wagenseil would have believed Bochart had stronger reasons not persuaded him the word means a kind of plant. From all this, Clarke says, the reader may take whichever opinion he likes best, or invent one of his own. His own is that mules were unknown before Anah, who either first crossed the mare with the ass or first met with such creatures in some very secluded corner of the wilderness — and he cannot resist a further conjecture, that the Enetae, whom Homer makes famous for a breed of wild mules where Pylaemenes ruled the Paphlagonians, may have taken their fabulous descent from this same Anah. Those people bordered on Paphlagonia, Cappadocia and Galatia, and Theophrastus, Strabo and Plutarch report that the first mules were seen among them.

Ellicott decides the other way and thinks it settled. Mules is the traditional Jewish rendering, but horses were unknown in Palestine at this date, so Anah cannot have discovered how to cross them with asses; and Jerome records that in Punic, a language akin to Hebrew, the word means hot springs — a translation now generally adopted. He points to Lange's list of hot springs in the Edomite country, and picks out those of Calirrhoe, the stream of beauty, in the Wady Zerka Maion, as likely to be the ones Anah came upon.

Calvin reads the verse as the mule-translation has it and turns it into a reproof. Mules are the adulterous offspring of horse and ass, and Anah is named as the author of the connection; but Calvin will not take that for praise of the man's industry, since God did not distinguish the kinds of animals from the beginning for nothing. The vanity of the flesh forever pushes the children of this world to busy themselves with superfluous things, and Moses marks an unnatural pursuit in a man not content with a great stock of animals unless he could add a degenerate race got by unnatural coupling. There is more moderation among brutes, Calvin concludes, in keeping the law of their nature than among men, who invent vicious mixtures.

Wesley takes the same clause as a compliment: Anah was industrious and ingenious besides, and successful — he found mules, or as some read it waters, hot baths, in the wilderness, and those diligent in their business sometimes find greater advantages than they looked for. Gill, keeping to the frame of the list, notes only that Zibeon was Seir's third son.
31:
That the crown here was not inherited is the one point the whole company agrees on, each reaching it by a different road. Keil and Delitzsch reason from the list itself: the eight follow one another, none coming to the throne until his predecessor is dead, yet no son succeeds his father, every man belongs to a different family and town, and of the last the notice that he died is missing. The sovereignty was therefore elective, the kings chosen by the phylarchs — and, they add, reigning alongside them, since Moses treats with a king of Edom about passage through the land while his own song makes the princes tremble. Gill reaches the same conclusion from Bishop Cumberland, who took these for Horite kings setting up a monarchy after their defeat by Chedorlaomer, to be better secured against another such disaster; he cites Maimonides for the observation that not one of them was an Edomite. Henry and Wesley credit the arrangement to bishop Patrick, and note that the country had by degrees passed out of Horite hands into Edomite ones.

Ellicott fills in the period between. The song at the sea still knows dukes of Edom, and by the time Israel reached the borders Edom had a king; so these were probably petty monarchs thrown up in different quarters during a long civil war, in which the Horites were as thoroughly beaten as the Canaanites afterwards under Saul and Solomon. Horite dukes of Seir's line had ruled districts mixed in among those of Esau's descendants, and now they vanish altogether.

The clause about Israel's kings is what unsettles Clarke, who thinks the whole passage down to the last king was transferred here out of Chronicles, since Moses can hardly have written it. He offers a mechanism: the succession was noted early in the margin of some authentic copy, to fill out the Edomite line before Saul was consecrated, and a later transcriber, taking a marginal entry for a repaired omission, wrote it into his text — as happened often enough, he says, glosses and restorations alike passing into the text of the Vulgate and Septuagint, and in a fourteenth-century English Bible lying before him. He knows the alternative, that king may mean any settled government by chiefs, dukes or judges, so that Moses meant only that Edom had rulers before Jacob's family grew powerful; he does not find it satisfactory. Esau, he reckons, had eight kings after his dukes, reigning while Israel was afflicted in Egypt.

Henry and Wesley take the sequence as doctrine. God had lately promised Jacob that kings should come of his loins, and Esau's blood turns royal long before any of Jacob's — for in outward prosperity the children of the covenant are often cast behind and those outside the covenant get the start. The triumphing of the wicked is quick but short, Henry says, soon ripe and as soon rotten, while the products of the promise are slow but sure. He then reads the return to dukes as a demotion: either the Edomites copied the Horite form, or providence reduced them to it to punish their refusing Israel a road through their country. When power is abused it is just with God to weaken it by splitting it into channels; for the transgression of a land many are the princes thereof, and sin brought Edom from kings to dukes, from crowns to coronets. Calvin puts the same lesson in his own figure. Reprobates are lifted suddenly that they may fall at once, like the herb on the housetop, rootless, quick to spring and quicker to wither; both sons of Isaac were promised kings, and Idumea began first, so that Israel looked the poorer — but time taught how much better it is to creep along the ground striking root deep than to hold a moment's extravagant pre-eminence.
32:
The first king needs guarding from two men he is not. Gill warns that the Greek spelling of his name invites confusion with Balak of Moab, and that some in Aben Ezra took him for the Balaam who was likewise a son of Beor but lived ages afterwards. Beyond his being the first of these Horite kings, and a date from Bedford, Gill says we know no more than the verse tells us; nor is it known how long he reigned, or whether he left sons, since none of them followed him on the throne.

The second raises the oldest guess in the chapter. Many have supposed him the Job of the book of afflictions and patience, and the Eliphaz of the earlier verses the friend who came to visit him; Clarke reports the identification and refuses it — there is no proper proof of it, and many reasons against. Ellicott dismisses it in a line, noting that the Greek translators made it on no probable grounds.

Of the rest, one is credited with a victory nobody can now trace. Clarke passes on Bishop Cumberland's conjecture that the Midian smitten in the field of Moab was Midian the son of Abraham by Keturah, killed before he was a hundred and nine, and that Moses recorded the stroke because it fell on an ancestor of his own father-in-law Jethro. Ellicott takes the opposite lesson from the same silence: every memory of the exploit has perished, and the Bible's complete silence about all these kings suggests they belong to a period earlier than the time when Israel began keeping careful record of events.

Two other names carry a note. Rehoboth by the river is literally Rehoboth-of-the-river, distinguished, Ellicott thinks, from the other Rehoboth; and if the river meant is the Euphrates, then the town lay outside Edomite ground and its king probably held Idumea by right of conquest. The last name he would correct to Hadad, the form the Samaritan text gives here and the Hebrew gives in Chronicles, the two Hebrew letters being so alike that they are repeatedly confused — and this, he reminds us, is the king who seems to have been still living when the catalogue was drawn up.

Gill's own contribution through these verses is a chronology, taken from Bedford: a date of death for each king in turn, with the note that one of them died better than forty years after the death of Abraham.
40:
A second set of dukes closes the chapter, and Gill is careful to keep them apart from the first. After the monarchy ceased the government reverted to dukes, of whom there were two races — the earlier drawn partly from Seir's line and partly from Esau's, holding office not by succession but side by side, each over his own family. He notices which names are missing from that earlier list: neither Esau himself nor his sons by the two first wives are called dukes, only the three sons of the last wife, all the rest being grandsons — a detail he thinks throws light on when the dukedoms began. His guess is that the joint weight of the two intermarried houses put an end to the regal power, and that they governed in this fashion for a course of years; and he marks the change of formula, the earlier men being dukes in the land of Edom while these later ones are something else.

Clarke limits their authority. They did not govern the whole Idumean nation but were chiefs in their own families and in their own places, the districts they ruled and gave their names to; and he passes on Calmet's opinion that the men named here were the dukes in office at the time Israel came out of Egypt.

Ellicott reads the list as a map. It is territorial — which does not mean the men were fictions, but that Edom finally settled into eleven thousands called after these chieftains, exactly as the names of Jacob's sons became the names of districts in Canaan, two of them going to Joseph's sons while none was called after Levi. What strikes him is the scale of the change. Not one Horite duke has left his name on any division of the country. Leaving out the disputed name, there were thirteen tribal princes at first, each with a territory and no central government over them — much as Israel lived for centuries in Canaan, each tribe independent in its district with nothing but religion to bind them. Here there are eleven, and only two, Teman and Kenaz, still carry the names of Esau's sons; of the other nine nothing is known, though we may safely conclude that they rose during the troubled years when one king after another seized the crown and was displaced. Many such men probably appeared, and these are simply the ones who consolidated power enough to leave a name behind. Through all that anarchy Teman and Kenaz alone held together, still ruled by princes of the one family. He adds a caution about the word family, which in Hebrew means a larger division of a tribe, subdivided into fathers' houses and again into households; and he would render the closing word not habitations but settlements.

Gill locates what he can of the names, mostly out of Jerome. Aholibamah, a woman's name earlier, is here a man's and also his district — Oolibama being a city of the princes of Edom. Elath was a country of those princes and a city of Esau, ten miles east of Petra; the seat of Pinon was very probably Phinon, lying between Petra and Zoar. Of the next three he observes that a Kenaz and a Teman had already appeared as dukes among the sons of Eliphaz, but takes these for different men, though the second may have been duke of the town named from the first — in Jerome's day a village five miles from Petra with a Roman garrison. Mabsar he identifies with the large village Mabsara in Gabalena, a part of Idumea, belonging to Petra. Keil and Delitzsch let the list stand as it is.
43:
The last name drew a long Jewish tradition after it. Gill reports from Jerome that Magdiel lay in Gabalena, once held by the dukes of Edom, and from the Targum of Jonathan that the duke took his name from his city, a strong migdal or tower; then Jarchi's gloss — this is Rome — and the saying among Jewish writers that Esau had a hundred provinces from Seir to Magdiel.

The closing formula Gill takes as a claim of full title. The earlier dukes were dukes in the land of Edom, sojourners there, or at least not the only dukes there, men of Seir's race holding rank beside them; these later ones, having driven the Horites out, were sole possessors and lords. So it stood, he observes, while Israel's posterity were sojourners in a strange land. Wesley makes the same contrast the moral of the register: Israel in the house of bondage with Canaan only promised, the Edomites in their own habitations with Seir in possession — for the children of this world have all in hand and nothing in hope, and the children of God often all in hope and next to nothing in hand. All things considered, he says, it is better to have Canaan in promise than mount Seir in possession.

Clarke closes the history and defends the man, nothing more of Esau appearing in the Pentateuch, and he a fixture in polemic divinity. Apart from selling the birthright and threatening his brother, the record is clean: hunger and Jacob's hard bargain account for the first, and the second, uttered in heat, he never tried to carry out though he had every means and opportunity. He then quotes Shuckford. Esau was plain, generous and honest, no worse than other men of his time, his good temper showing through his whole conduct toward his brother — all humanity at their meeting, no resentment when Jacob settled near his father instead of following him, and no difficulty at Isaac's death about leaving Canaan, the point that would have revived any grudge he was nursing. Scripture calls him profane and says Esau have I hated; but the sentence was passed before the children had done good or evil, and the hatred brought no punishment, since he was as happy in this life as Abraham or Jacob, and his posterity held a land God assigned them, entered it before Israel entered theirs, and were shielded by a strict warning against invasion — so why not find him at the last day with Lot or Job? All he lost was the inheritance of the promise, which Lot and Job never had; and Paul's argument only shows that God bestowed the favours leading to the Messiah where he pleased. Profane, Shuckford adds, does not mean wicked, but marks a man who set no due value on the priest's office. Clarke's summary is blunt: the Messiah had to come through one family, and God chose Abraham's line through Isaac and Jacob rather than Ishmael or Esau — from which it does not follow that the first were all saved and the others lost.

He ends with a defence of the genealogies. Registering Esau's descent was as necessary as Jacob's, precisely to show the Messiah did not spring from it; and such tables, little regarded now, prove the prophecies naming one family fulfilled, and answer the Jews out of Jesus of Nazareth, sprung from David's last branch. The registers were kept till Jerusalem fell and destroyed with it, so that no Jew alive can trace himself to David — which leaves any Messiah still to come without legitimate birth. When Christ came, and when Matthew and Luke wrote, the rolls still existed; had the evangelists claimed what could not be supported, an appeal to them would have convicted the claim. None was made, and because none was, Clarke reasons, none could be made.
